14: The order of portions and prophetic readings that are read and concluded throughout the year, from the end of Sukkot until the end of the next Sukkot, every sabbath having one portion and one prophetic readings.
V-Eleh Shmot: Jeremiah 1:1–2:3. Some conclude with Ezekiel 16:1–14. Some conclude with Isaiah 27:5–16.
Bo El Par'o: Jeremiah 46:13–28. Some conclude with Isaiah 19:1–25.
V-Eleh HaMishpaṭim: Jeremiah 34:8–22, ending with Jeremiah 33:25
Tsav Et Aharon: Jeremiah 7:21–28, ending with Jeremiah 9:22–23
Aḥarei Mot: Amos 8:18–9:15. Some conclude with Ezekiel 22:2–16.

And we are told in the Pesiqta, from Bereshit until the 17th of Tammuz we conclude with something related to the matter of the portions. From there on, everything goes according to the time and according to the scenario: three of rebuke and seven of comfort and two of repentance. And their mnemonic is DShḤ NV' ARQ ShDSh.
Eleh HaDvarim, before the ninth of Av: Ḥazon Yesha'yahu, Isaiah 1:1–27.
VaEtḥanan (the seven of comfort, NV' ARQ Sh): Naḥamu, Isaiah 40:1–26.

R'eh Anokhi: 'Uri 'Uri, Isaiah 51:9–52:10.noteOr alternatively, 52:1–10. Both verses start with the same two words, but 51:9 is cited below. Some printings add here: "Some conclude with Isaiah 54:11–55:5." This is the practice in nearly every community today
V-Haya Ki Tavo: Qumi Ori, Isaiah 60:1–22.
Atem Nitsavim, before Rosh haShanah: Sos Asis, Isaiah 61:10–63:9.

VaYelekh, during the ten days between Rosh haShanah and Yom Kippur (the two of repentance, DSh) — Dirshu, Isaiah 55:6-56:8. And this is what we said in Tractate Rosh haShanah 18a:10–12 — "seek the LORD where he can be found" for an individual, but "like the LORD our God whenever we call out to Him" (Deut. 4:7) for the community. For an individual, when? During the ten days between Rosh haShanah and Yom Kippur.

Ha'azinu after Yom Kippur: Shuva Yisrael, Hosea 14:2–10, ending with Micah 7:18–20. And if you would say "what benefit is repentance after Yom Kippur?" one can respond in the name of what R. Yitzḥaq said: crying out is good for a person both before the judgment and after it. (Rosh haShanah 16a:13).

And in most places in Spain, on the sabbath of the ten days of repentance they conclude with Hosea 14:2–10, and on the sabbath after Yom Kippur with I Samuel 22:1–51. But thisnote"This" in this case being what every community does today is impossible, because this prophetic reading is not on a matter of repentance, and one must say the second of the two of repentance, as we said. And this is written in the order of Rabbeinu Tam, and I also heard it is the custom in France and Provence. And Rabbeinu Saadia wrote that on the sabbath between Rosh haShanah and Yom Kippur one must conclude with Isaiah 55:6-56:8.

And know that some of these prophetic readings are sometimes replaced with other prophetic readings, for instance if a new moon falls on the sabbath or Sunday. But the prophetic readings of DShḤ NV' ARQ ShDSh. are never replaced with another ever.

And the Midrash punningly says that they established to say at the beginning of the prophetic readings of consolation "Comfort, comfort my people" (Isaiah 40:1) — that is to say, the Holy Blessed One said to the prophets, "Comfort, comfort my people!" Upon this the congregation of Israel responds, "But Zion says, 'the LORD has abandoned me!'" (Isaiah 49:14) that is to say, "I cannot be reconciled to the comfort of the prophets." And it says "Rise, rise, dress in strength, arm of the LORD; rise as days of old!" (Isaiah 51:9). And in places where it they conclude in place of this prophetic reading "Unhappy, storm-tossed" (Isaiah 54:11), it is as if to say the prophets respond and say before the Holy Blessed One, "Lo, the congregation of Israel is not reconciled to our comforting!" Upon this the Holy Blessed One responds and says, "I, I myself will comfort you" (Isaiah 51:12), and what's more, "Rejoice, barren one without children" (Isaiah 54:1), and what's more, "Rise, shine, for your light has come!" (Isaiah 60:1). To this, the congregation of Israel responds, "I will rejoice, rejoicing in the LORD" (Isaiah 61:10), that is to say, now I have something to rejoice and celebrate! "My soul will cheer in my God, who clad me in clothing of salvation" etc.

Rabbeinu Saadia wrote: a sabbath where there is mourning for a sage, conclude with the portion of I Samuel 4:1–22. And I found written in a responsa asked to the rabbi Shmuel ben Gershon, and this was his word and what was told to you, that when the Rambam of blessed memory passed away, when the congregation was gathered to the synagogue, they read the blessings and curses, and concluded prophetically with "Moses My servant is dead" (Joshua 1:2). Thus we have also heard, that Abba Mari of blessed memory wrote in his laws of mourning: when Rabbeinu Sherira, the father of Rabbeinu Hai, died, they read that Sabbath the portion of Numbers 27:15–23, and concluded with I Kings 2:1–21, but in place of the verse "And Solomon sat on the throne of David his father" they read "and Hai sat on the throne of Sherira his father, and his reign was greatly established."

The sabbath on which they read two portions, for instance VaYaqhel with Eleh Fqudei, or Isha Ki Tazria with Zot Tihyeh, in most communities in Spain they conclude with the prophetic reading of the first portion, that is to say, the portion of VaYaqhel or of Isha Ki Tazria. But some places they conclude with the prophetic reading of the second portion, because it ends with it. And thus wrote the Rambam of blessed memory.

And when a festival falls on the sabbath day, they read according to the matter of the festival and not per the order of the sabbath, and so too they read a prophetic reading of the festival. Nevertheless, one does not read in the afternoon of the sabbath prior or the Monday and Thursday prior the beginning of the portion for the festival, but rather the beginning of the portion for the sabbath, and they will return to the start of that portion on the week after the festival, after reading it the week before the festival. Thus it can so occur that they read the opening of VaYhi BaYom HaShmini seven times, and this is when Passover falls on the sabbath, so they read the beginning of the portion in the afternoon of the sabbath prior, and Monday and Thursday before Passover, and the afternoon of the sabbath of the first day of the festival, and the afternoon of the sabbath of the last day of the festival, and Monday and Thursday afterwards. And so too it can occur that they read the opening of V-Zot HaBrakha four times, and this is when Sukkot falls on the sbabbath, so they read the beginning of the portion the afternoon of that the sabbath and the Thursday before Sukkot (since they wouldn't read it on Monday since it is Yom Kippur) and they read it on the afternoon of the sabbath of the first day of the festival, and the afternoon of the sabbath of the last day of the festival, since Simḥat Torah is the first day after that.
